title: FOMC Minutes — January 27–28, 2026
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2026-01-28 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

With Jerome Powell chairing, the Committee held the federal funds target range at 3.50–3.75%. Interest on reserve balances stayed at 3.65% and the primary credit rate at 3.75%. The vote was 10–2. Stephen Miran and Christopher Waller dissented in favor of a quarter-point cut. They saw policy as "still meaningfully restrictive" and judged downside labor market risks to be the bigger concern.

Economic outlook

The staff forecast was stronger than in December. Real GDP growth was expected to run above potential through 2028, and unemployment was expected to fall below the staff's natural-rate estimate by year-end. Staff saw risks to growth and employment tilted to the downside.

Inflation

Inflation stayed above target. Tariffs pushed up core goods prices, while housing-led disinflation in services continued. PCE and core PCE were both 2.8% in November. CPI was 2.7% in December and core CPI 2.6%. Staff raised their inflation forecast slightly and expected tariff effects to fade from mid-2026. Most participants warned that progress toward 2% "might be slower and more uneven than generally expected." Staff called persistence a salient upside risk. Longer-term expectations were consistent with 2%.

Labor market

Unemployment was 4.4% in December and had held steady. Hiring, layoffs and job gains were all low. Most participants saw signs that the labor market was stabilizing and thought downside risks had eased, though some pointed to softer survey readings. Participants also discussed AI's effect on hiring and lower net immigration, which slows labor supply.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Markets priced in one to two 25bp cuts for 2026. Equity valuations were high, although the largest tech firms underperformed. Staff rated financial vulnerabilities as notable and asset valuation pressures as elevated. The dollar weakened. The Desk's yen "rate checks" were done only on behalf of the Treasury, and there was no FX intervention. Reserve management purchases of Treasury bills (plus Treasuries maturing in three years or less if needed) continued, with reserves expected to stay near $3 trillion. Usage of the standing repo facility rose after the December changes. Year-end money market pressures were subdued.

Risks participants flagged

  • Stickier inflation from tariffs and strong demand
  • A sharp labor market downturn in a low-hiring environment
  • Exposures to private credit and nonbanks, hedge fund leverage and Treasury market fragility
  • AI-related valuations, market concentration and debt financing
  • Strain on low- and middle-income households, plus spillovers from global bond and currency volatility

What it signaled about next moves

Several participants expected more cuts if inflation fell as projected. Some preferred to hold "for some time" until disinflation was clearer. Several would have supported two-sided guidance that left room for hikes. Everyone agreed policy was "not on a preset course."

Read-through for SPY

  • The Fed held rates with a mild easing bias, and markets still expected one or two cuts in 2026. That was supportive, but no help was coming right away.
  • The staff upgraded growth, which is good for earnings. But the Fed itself called stock valuations high and flagged AI concentration as a risk.
  • Hints of two-sided (possible hike) guidance were an early warning that sticky inflation could take rate cuts off the table.
